The problem: IMO 2026 Problem 4, answer θ = 180/n for integer n ≥ 2.

The write-up states: "Mulan wins uniformly iff θ=180/n, n≥2 integer." That's the correct answer. Field "answer": 2 if explicit and correct. Yes, section 5 states θ = 180°/n for integer n ≥ 2. So answer = 2.

"reduction" = (K): a preparatory lemma "if the current triangle has an angle equal to kθ for some integer k ≥ 1, Mulan wins" by induction on k, splitting kθ into θ + (k-1)θ so both pieces carry an integer multiple of θ, or an equivalent tool.

Section 2: "Multiples become universally winning": If kθ < 180 then kθ is universally winning and triangles containing kθ ⊂ W_{k-1}. Indeed kθ = (k-1)θ + θ. Explicit decrease: if T contains kθ ≥ 2θ, cutting kθ as θ + (k-1)θ yields C1 with θ, C2 with (k-1)θ. Whichever Shan-Yu keeps, either Mulan wins immediately or new triangle contains (k-1)θ.

Wait — I need to check the cut model. The move: Mulan chooses a point P on perimeter, cuts from P to the opposite vertex. Given triangle with angles (p, q, D), choosing donor D means... Let me think: cutting from the vertex of angle D to a point on the opposite side (the side between the vertices with angles p and q). Then the two children: one has angles (p, x, 180 - p - x) where x is the angle at the point... hmm, actually the model: children (p, x, 180-p-x) and (q, D-x, p+x). Let me verify: triangle with vertices A, B, C with angles p at A, q at B, D at C. Cut from C to point P on AB. Let angle ACP = x, then angle PCB = D - x. Triangle ACP: angles p (at A), x (at C), 180 - p - x (at P). Triangle PCB: angles q (at B), D - x (at C), and at P: 180 - q - (D - x) = 180 - q - D + x = p + x (since p + q + D = 180). Yes, the model (1) is correct: C1 = (p, x, 180-p-x), C2 = (q, D-x, p+x). And 180 - p - x = q + D - x. Good.

Now for the split D = θ + (k-1)θ: cutting donor D with x = θ gives C1 = (p, θ, 180 - p - θ), which contains θ; C2 = (q, D - θ, p + θ) = (q, (k-1)θ, p+θ), which contains (k-1)θ. Both pieces carry an integer multiple of θ (piece 1 contains θ = 1·θ, piece 2 contains (k-1)θ). Need x = θ ∈ (0, D): since D = kθ with k ≥ 2, θ < kθ = D, so x = θ is feasible. Good. So the induction: triangle containing kθ is in W_{k-1}. This is (K) essentially — a lemma "if the current triangle has an angle equal to kθ, Mulan wins" proved by induction on k with both pieces carrying integer multiples. Actually the write-up proves "triangles containing kθ ⊂ W_{k-1}", which is exactly the induction on k. So reduction = 2? The rubric says (K) is "a preparatory lemma of the kind ... or an equivalent tool such as a cut lemma with an existence argument for the required cut point". The write-up has this: Section 2 with the induction. The existence of the cut point: x = θ with 0 < θ < D = kθ, fine. So reduction = 2.

"lower_bound" = (W): Mulan wins for θ = 180/n against every initial triangle and every discard choice, including n = 2 case and mechanism guaranteeing after each cut both pieces are winning positions.

Section 1 handles θ = 90°: every triangle is in W1. Let me check the argument: T has angles p ≤ q ≤ D. At least two are acute, pick p, q < 90. Then p > 0 and q < 90 implies D + p = 180 - q > 90, so r := 90 - p satisfies 0 < r < D. Wait, need r < D: r = 90 - p < D ⟺ 90 < D + p ⟺ 180 - q > 90 ⟺ q < 90. Yes. Splitting D as r and D - r gives C1 = (p, 90 - p, 180 - p - (90-p)) = (p, 90-p, 90). C2 = (q, D - r, p + r) = (q, D - 90 + p, 90). Both contain 90. So Mulan wins in one move for θ = 90. That's correct. Actually, wait: cutting the donor D (largest angle) with x = r = 90 - p: C1 = (p, x, 180 - p - x) = (p, 90-p, 90). Yes contains 90. C2 = (q, D - x, p + x) = (q, D - 90 + p, p + 90 - p) = (q, D - 90 + p, 90). Contains 90. Good. And x ∈ (0, D): 0 < r since p < 90 (p is acute, being one of two smallest angles which are acute). Good.

Section 3: θ = 180/n, n ≥ 3. Any triangle containing a multiple is in W_{n-2} by (2). Let T contain no angle from M = {θ, ..., (n-1)θ}. Every triangle has an angle ≤ 60°; choose p minimal, p ≤ 60°, p ∉ M. Write p = kθ + α with 0 < α < θ (p not a multiple so α ≠ 0; also p > 0 so kθ + α with α ∈ (0, θ), k ≥ 0). Then r = (k+1)θ - p = θ - α ∈ (0, θ), and p + r = (k+1)θ. Need (k+1)θ ∈ M, i.e., (k+1)θ < 180 and k+1 ≥ 1 obviously. Since p ≤ 60° and r < θ ≤ 60°, p + r ≤ 60 + θ ≤ 120 < 180. And (k+1)θ = p + r is a multiple of θ which is < 180, so it's in M. Good.

Let D be a maximal angle, D ≥ 60° ≥ r; indeed r < θ ≤ 60° ≤ D; also D ∉ M so D > r... "so x = r is feasible". We need 0 < r < D: r > 0, r < θ ≤ 60 ≤ D. Good. Cutting D as r and D - r:

C1 = (p, r, 180 - p - r) where 180 - p - r = 180 - (k+1)θ = (n - k - 1)θ. Need this to be in M: (n-k-1)θ is a positive multiple of θ, positive? p + r = (k+1)θ ≤ 120 < 180 so n - k - 1 ≥ 1? (k+1)θ < 180 = nθ means k+1 < n, i.e., k+1 ≤ n-1, so n - k - 1 ≥ 1. Yes positive. So C1 contains (n-k-1)θ ∈ M. Good.

C2 = (q, D - r, p + r) with p + r = (k+1)θ ∈ M. Good.

Both children contain multiples of θ, hence both in W_{n-2}. So T ∈ W_{n-1}. The strategy: if triangle contains kθ with k ≥ 2, cut into θ + (k-1)θ; Shan-Yu loses or k drops. If contains no multiple, do the p-minimal D-maximal cut; both children contain multiples, so after this move in previous case with k ≤ n - 1. After at most n - 1 moves θ appears.

Hmm, let me count: if T contains no multiple, one move to reach a triangle containing kθ with k ≤ n - 1 (since any multiple in M has k ≤ n - 1). Then k - 1 more moves at most. Total ≤ 1 + (n - 2) = n - 1. Fine.

This covers every initial triangle (both cases: contains a multiple or not) and every discard choice (both children are winning positions — that's the W_{k} definition requiring C1, C2 ∈ W_k). The n = 2 case is handled. So lower_bound = 2.

But wait — I should double-check the claim "Any triangle containing a multiple is already in W_{n-2} by (2)". (2) says triangles containing kθ ⊂ W_{k-1} for kθ < 180. In the divisor case, multiples are kθ for 1 ≤ k ≤ n-1, so triangles containing kθ are in W_{k-1} ⊆ W_{n-2}. Good.

One subtlety in Section 2: "If s, s' are universally winning at level k and s + s' < 180, then s+s' is universally winning at level k+1: any T = (p, q, s+s') with x = s gives C1 containing s, C2 containing s'..." Let me verify: donor D = s + s', x = s ∈ (0, D). C1 = (p, s, ...) contains s — wait, C1 = (p, x, 180 - p - x) = (p, s, 180 - p - s) contains s. C2 = (q, D - x, p + x) = (q, s', p + s) contains s'. Both children contain universally winning angles, so they're in W_k (universally winning at level k means every triangle containing that angle is in W_k). So T ∈ W_{k+1}. Correct.

Then inductively kθ universally winning at level k-1. Base: θ universally winning at level 0 (W_0 = triangles containing θ). Inductive step: (k-1)θ at level k-2 and θ at level 0, so kθ at level max(k-2, 0) + 1 = k-1 for k ≥ 2. The write-up states triangles containing kθ ⊂ W_{k-1} "with W_0 for k=1". Fine.

So the reduction (K) = 2, lower bound (W) = 2.

"upper_bound" = (A): Shan-Yu avoids θ forever for θ not 180/n against every cut.

Section 4: δ := 180 mod θ ∈ (0, θ). M = {kθ : 1 ≤ k ≤ m, kθ < 180}, I = triangles with no angle in M. Since M finite, I ≠ ∅: choose a ∉ M small, choose b ∉ M with 180 - a - b ∉ M. For each value of k, the constraints "b = 180 - a - kθ" pin down at most one b (finitely many forbidden b values from the third condition), and b ∉ M excludes finitely many more. The interval (0, 180 - a) is infinite, so there's a valid b. The write-up is a bit terse but asserts existence. Is it written out as a complete argument? It's terse: "Since M finite, I ≠ ∅: choose a ∉ M small, choose b ∉ M with 180 - a - b ∉ M." Hmm, this just asserts it. I'd say this is acceptable — it's a one-line existence with clear reasoning implied. But strictly, the write-up doesn't spell out the finiteness of the forbidden set for b. Hmm. So choosing b avoiding finitely many forbidden values in an infinite interval. The write-up says "choose b ∉ M with 180-a-b ∉ M" — this presupposes such b exists, which needs the finiteness argument. I think this is a minor gap but arguably the reader can fill it in trivially. Grading rubric: "A mechanism scored 2 must be written out as a complete argument covering every opponent choice". The core of (A) is the lemma: if T ∈ I then for any cut at least one child ∈ I.

The lemma proof: T = (p, q, D) ∈ I, p, q, D ∉ M. Children in (1). New angles in C1: x and 180 - p - x (p is old, p ∉ M). New angles in C2: D - x and p + x (q old). If both children ∉ I, then C1 has an angle in M: x = k1θ or 180 - p - x = k1θ. C2: D - x = k2θ or p + x = k3θ.

Case 1: x = k1θ and D - x = k2θ ⇒ D = (k1 + k2)θ ∈ M. Contradiction. ✓.
Case 2: x = k1θ and p + x = k3θ ⇒ p = (k3 - k1)θ, a multiple (or zero if k3 = k1, impossible as p > 0). Hmm, wait: if k3 - k1 ≥ 1, then p ∈ M provided p < 180, which holds since p is an angle. Actually p = (k3 - k1)θ; since p > 0, k3 > k1, so p is a positive multiple of θ, and p < 180, so p ∈ M. Contradiction with p ∉ M. ✓.
Case 3: 180 - p - x = k1θ and D - x = k2θ ⇒ subtract: 180 - p - D = (k1 - k2)θ, i.e., q = (k1 - k2)θ. Since q > 0, k1 > k2, so q ∈ M. Contradiction. ✓.
Case 4: 180 - p - x = k1θ and p + x = k3θ ⇒ sum: 180 = (k1 + k3)θ. But 180 is not a multiple of θ (δ ≠ 0). Contradiction. ✓.

Wait — case 4: (k1 + k3)θ = 180 means 180 is an integer multiple of θ. Given the non-divisor assumption, contradiction. But hold on: this is where the hypothesis "180 not a multiple of θ" is used exactly, as the rubric describes. ✓.

Actually wait, there's a subtlety: in case 4, k1 + k3 ≥ 2 obviously since both ≥ 1. Fine.

So the lemma is correctly proven, covering every donor choice and every x ∈ (0, D). Then the consequence: Shan-Yu starts with T0 ∈ I, and after every Mulan cut chooses the child in I. The game never hits an angle in M, in particular never θ. So Mulan never wins. This covers every Mulan play. ✓.

Also handles θ > 90°: M = {θ} (since 2θ > 180), and case analysis shows W1 = W0 — the lemma covers all θ with 180 not a multiple of θ, including θ > 90. Fine.

So upper_bound = 2. The existence of initial triangle in I is slightly terse but I think acceptable. Let me reconsider: "Since M finite, I ≠ ∅: choose a ∉ M small, choose b ∉ M with 180-a-b ∉ M." The justification "M finite" is given. Given a ∉ M (exists since (0,180) infinite, M finite), the set of b to avoid: M and {180 - a - m : m ∈ M}, both finite; (0, 180 - a) is an interval with infinitely many reals. So such b exists. Hmm, but let me double check the claim in Section 2 more carefully: "Inductively, if kθ < 180 then kθ is universally winning and (2)". Also "Let m = ⌊180/θ⌋, M = {kθ : 1 ≤ k ≤ m, kθ < 180}". Options: x = θ & D - x = θ ⇒ D = 2θ; x = θ & p + x = θ ⇒ p = 0 impossible; 180 - p - x = θ & D - x = θ ⇒ q = 0 impossible (they wrote "180-p-θ = θ + q?" — a bit garbled but concluded q = 0 impossible; correct: 180 - p - x = θ means q + D - x = θ; with D - x = θ, q = 0); 180 - p - x = θ & p + x = θ ⇒ 180 = 2θ. So for θ ≠ 90, the only way is D = 2θ. ✓. This section isn't strictly needed for the final proof but it's fine.

Now check the lower bound strategy once more for n ≥ 3, specifically the case where T contains a multiple kθ, k ≥ 2: cut donor kθ with x = θ: C1 = (p, θ, 180 - p - θ) contains θ → immediate win if kept. C2 = (q, (k-1)θ, p + θ) contains (k-1)θ. If k - 1 = 1, C2 contains θ → win. Else descend. And in the "no multiple" case, the cut produces C1 containing (n-k-1)θ and C2 containing (k+1)θ, both in M hence both in W_{n-2}. So whichever Shan-Yu keeps, Mulan wins within n-2 more moves. One more check: in the no-multiple case, feasibility x = r requires r < D where D is a maximal angle. r < θ ≤ 60° and D ≥ 60°. If θ = 60° (n = 3), then r < θ = 60 ≤ D, so r < D strictly. ✓.
